questions.question: What is one of the primary roles of international organisations (IOS) in resolving international conflicts?

options.text: To escalate violence for faster conflict resolution
To act as neutral arenas for diplomacy, mediation, and humanitarian intervention
To prevent the formation of treaties between states
To limit communication between conflicting states

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The passage explicitly identifies the role of IOs in the very first sentence: **"acting as key arenas for diplomacy, mediation, and humanitarian intervention."**
 
• It further explains that these organisations provide **"neutral environments"** where states can communicate and resolve conflicts without resorting to violence.
 
• Why other options are incorrect: 
 
 
• **Option 1:** The text states IOs help states resolve conflicts **"without resorting to violence,"** which is the opposite of escalating it.
 
• **Option 3:** The passage says IOs allow states to **"make treaties,"** not prevent them.
 
• **Option 4:** The text highlights that IOs provide a platform where **"states can communicate,"** thereby facilitating rather than limiting communication.
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **2**.

 

**Analytical Insight:** *In exams, reading comprehension questions on international relations often focus on the "functional" purpose of institutions. The keyword here is **"Neutral,"** which is the primary value proposition of an IO in a conflict scenario.*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mediation:** Intervention in a dispute in order to resolve it; arbitration.
 
• **Multilateral:** Agreed upon or participated in by three or more parties, especially the governments of different countries.
 
• **Geopolitical:** Relating to politics, especially international relations, as influenced by geographical factors.
 
• **Veto Power:** The power or right vested in one branch of a government or a specific member (like the P5 in the UN) to cancel or postpone the decisions of another.

questions.question: How do international organisations contribute to post-conflict stability, as mentioned in the passage?

questions.question:
**Change the following sentence into the Active form.**

The championship game was won by our team.

options.text: Our team won the championship game.
The championship game was winning our team. team.
Our team wins the championship game.
The championship game had been won by our team.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is '1' i.e. Our team won the championship game.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The given sentence is in the **passive voice**. Passive voice emphasizes the action or the object receiving the action rather than the subject performing it.
 
• To change a sentence from passive to active voice, identify the subject performing the action and place it at the beginning of the sentence.
 
• The structure of active voice is **Subject + Verb + Object**.
 
• In the sentence, "The championship game was won by our team," the subject performing the action is "our team," the verb is "won," and the object is "the championship game."

Correct sentence: *Our team won the championship game.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Passive Voice:**
 
 
• **Structure:** Object + to be (correct tense) + past participle + by + subject.
 
• **Example:** The book was read by the teacher.
 
• **Usage:** Used when the focus is on the action or the object receiving the action.
 
 
 
• **Active Voice:**
 
 
• **Structure:** Subject + Verb + Object.
 
• **Example:** The teacher read the book.
 
• **Usage:** Used when the focus is on the subject performing the action.
 
 
</ul

questions.question:

He will tell her, "I have already finished my work."

options.text: He will tell her that he had already finished his work.
He will tell her that he has already finished his work.
He will tell her that he already finished his work.
He will tell her that he would have finished his work.

questions.solution:

__
 
• In indirect speech, the tense of the verb generally changes depending on the tense of the reporting verb.
 
• Since the reporting verb in the sentence is in the future tense ("He will tell her"), the tense in the indirect speech remains unchanged for the present perfect tense.
 
• The direct speech sentence contains the present perfect tense: "I have already finished my work." In indirect speech, it remains "has already finished his work."
 
• Option 2 is correct because the tense and meaning align accurately with the rules of indirect speech.

Correct sentence: *He will tell her that he **has already finished** his work*.

• **Rules for Tense Change in Indirect Speech:**
 
 
• **Present Perfect → Remains Present Perfect** if the reporting verb is in the future tense.
 
• Example: "I have completed the task" → He will say that he has completed the task.
 
 
 
• **Common Errors:**
 
 
• Option 1: "Had already finished" changes the tense unnecessarily.
 
• Option 3: "Already finished" omits the auxiliary verb "has," making the sentence grammatically incorrect.
 
• Option 4: "Would have finished" incorrectly uses a conditional form not present in the original sentence.

questions.question:

__
 
• The given sentence is in the **present perfect tense** ("has written").
 
• To convert it to passive voice, the structure of the present perfect tense changes as follows:
 
 
• **Active voice:** Subject + has/have + past participle + object.
 
• **Passive voice:** Object + has/have + been + past participle + by + subject.

• **Option 4:** "An elegant and efficient code is written by the skilled programmer..." uses the present simple tense ("is written"), which is incorrect as the original sentence is in the present perfect tense.
 
 
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following article of the Indian constitution promotes equal justice and free legal aid?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 39 A**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 39A** of the **Indian Constitution** directs the state to ensure that the legal system promotes justice on the basis of equal opportunity and to provide free legal aid to economically weaker sections of society.
 
• This article was introduced by the **42nd Amendment Act of 1976** under the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP).
 
• It mandates the state to ensure that no citizen is denied access to justice due to economic or other disabilities.
 
• The provision emphasizes the importance of creating a fair and equitable judicial system accessible to all, irrespective of their financial status.
 
• The implementation of **free legal aid services** has been institutionalized through the **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987**, which established **National Legal Services Authority (NALSA)** to oversee legal aid programs.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP):**

 
 
• DPSPs are non-justiciable rights enshrined in Part IV of the Indian Constitution, aimed at guiding the state in governance and policy-making to establish a welfare state.
 
• These principles are inspired by the **Irish Constitution** and aim to promote social and economic justice.
 
• Though not enforceable in a court of law, they are fundamental in the governance of the country and are intended to be implemented by legislative and executive actions.
 
 
 
• **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987:**
 
 
• This act was enacted to provide free and competent legal services to weaker sections of society and to ensure justice for all.
 
• It led to the creation of institutions like **National Legal Services Authority (NALSA)** at the national level and **State Legal Services Authorities (SLSA)** at the state level.
 
• These institutions provide free legal aid, conduct Lok Adalats, and spread legal awareness.
 
 
 
• **Article 38:**
 
 
• Article 38 directs the state to strive to promote the welfare of the people by securing and protecting a social order based on justice, social, economic, and political.
 
• It focuses on minimizing inequalities in income, status, facilities, and opportunities among individuals and groups.
 
 
 
• **Other Related Articles:**
 
 
• **Article 45:** Originally directed the state to provide free and compulsory education for children below the age of 14; later amended to focus on early childhood care and education for children below six years.
 
• **Article 42:** Directs the state to make provisions for securing just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Role of NALSA:**

 
 
• NALSA was constituted under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, and works to provide free legal services to the weaker sections of society.
 
• It organizes **Lok Adalats** to resolve disputes through alternative dispute resolution mechanisms.
 
• NALSA also promotes legal awareness through campaigns and programs at the grassroots level.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Article 39A:**
 
 
• It is a cornerstone of India's commitment to ensuring justice for all.
 
• It reflects the constitutional vision of building an inclusive judicial system that does not discriminate against marginalized groups.
 
• Free legal aid under this article is a step toward achieving the goal of **social and economic justice**.
 
 
 
• **Global Perspective:**
 
 
• Many countries have similar provisions to ensure access to justice, such as the **Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders Act, 2012** in the **UK**.
 
• The **Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948)** also emphasizes the right to access justice without discrimination.

questions.question: Which of the following is correct regarding Sale of government assets like sale of shares in Public sector unit (PSU)?

options.text: It creates liability for the government
Amount comes from sale of shares are part of capital receipts
Amount comes from sale of shares are part of revenue receipts
It does not reduce the total assets of the government

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 2: Amount comes from the sale of shares are part of capital receipts.**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__
 

__ 
 
• **Sale of government assets like PSU shares** is categorized under **capital receipts** because it involves the realization of capital assets, such as equity, by the government. 
 
• The funds raised through the sale of shares in Public Sector Units (PSUs) are **non-recurring in nature** and do not constitute a regular source of income for the government. 
 
• The amount received from such sales is used to **reduce the fiscal deficit or fund developmental activities**, rather than being treated as revenue receipts. 
 
• **Revenue receipts** include recurring income such as taxes and duties, whereas proceeds from disinvestment represent a **capital inflow**. 
 
• The sale of government shares in PSUs does not create liability for the government; instead, it reduces its ownership in these entities while generating funds. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 

__ 
 
• **Capital Receipts:** 
 
 
• Capital receipts are those receipts that **result in either an increase in liabilities or a reduction in assets** of the government. 
 
• Examples include **loans raised by the government**, disinvestment proceeds, borrowings from external sources, and recovery of loans. 
 
• They are used to **finance capital expenditure** or manage fiscal deficits. 
 
 
 
• **Revenue Receipts:** 
 
 
• Revenue receipts are government receipts that **do not create liabilities or reduce assets**. 
 
• They consist of **tax revenues (income tax, GST, etc.) and non-tax revenues** (interest, dividends, and fees). 
 
• These are used to meet the recurring expenses of the government, such as salaries, subsidies, and maintenance costs. 
 
 
 
• **Disinvestment:** 
 
 
• Disinvestment refers to the **sale or liquidation of government-owned assets or shares in PSUs**. 
 
• The primary objectives of disinvestment are **to reduce the fiscal burden, improve public finances, and enhance operational efficiency** in PSUs. 
 
• For example, the government’s disinvestment in companies like Air India and BPCL has been part of its fiscal strategy. 
 
 
 
• **Fiscal Deficit:** 
 
 
• Fiscal deficit is the difference between the government’s total expenditure and total revenue (excluding borrowings). 
 
• Proceeds from disinvestment are often utilized to **bridge the fiscal deficit** and reduce the government’s reliance on borrowing. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 

 
 
• **Statement 1:** "It creates liability for the government" is **incorrect**. The sale of assets does not create liability; instead, it reduces ownership in PSUs. 
 
• **Statement 2:** "Amount comes from the sale of shares are part of capital receipts" is **correct**. Such inflows are capital receipts as they affect the capital structure of the government. 
 
• **Statement 3:** "Amount comes from the sale of shares are part of revenue receipts" is **incorrect**. Revenue receipts involve recurring income, unlike disinvestment proceeds. 
 
• **Statement 4:** "It does not reduce the total assets of the government" is **incorrect**. The sale of shares reduces the government’s shareholding, thereby reducing its assets.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Industrial Policy of 1991:** 
 

• The policy was introduced by the then Finance Minister **Dr. Manmohan Singh** under the leadership of Prime Minister **P. V. Narasimha Rao**. 

• It aimed to reduce the **bureaucratic control** over industries and boost private sector participation in industrial development. 

• The policy also emphasized **globalization**, **privatization**, and **liberalization** to enhance India's economic growth. 

• It allowed **foreign equity participation** up to a certain percentage in various sectors and permitted **FDI** in key industries.

• It acted as a **single-window clearance system** for FDI proposals requiring approval. 

• The FIPB was abolished in **2017** as part of the government's effort to simplify the FDI process, and its functions were transferred to **concerned ministries and departments**. 
 
 

• **Features of Industrial Policy 1991:** 
 

• **Delicensing:** Most industries were exempted from licensing except for a few sectors like defense and hazardous chemicals. 

• **Disinvestment:** It reduced the role of the public sector by allowing privatization of public enterprises. 

• **Trade Liberalization:** The policy removed restrictions on imports and exports, making the Indian economy more open to global markets. 

• **Technology Transfer:** It encouraged the adoption of advanced technologies and collaboration with foreign firms. 
 
 

• **Impact of 1991 Reforms:**

• The **excise duty structure** was rationalized in the **financial year 2001-02** to a single rate of **16 per cent CENVAT**, simplifying the previous complex multi-rate system. 

• **CENVAT (Central Value Added Tax)** replaced the traditional excise duty structure to ensure uniform taxation and reduce cascading effects on goods and services. 

• This reform aimed to bring **transparency**, enhance **compliance**, and create a simplified taxation regime for manufacturers and producers in India. 

• The single rate of **16 per cent CENVAT** facilitated easier calculation and administration of excise duties, benefiting industries and reducing bureaucratic hurdles. 

• This rationalization was also part of the broader efforts to modernize India's taxation system and align it with global practices.

__ 

• **Excise Duty:** 
 

• Excise duty is a **tax levied on the manufacture of goods within the country**, and it is collected by the government from manufacturers or producers. 

• It is an **indirect tax**, meaning the burden is ultimately passed on to the consumer. 

• In India, excise duties are governed by the **Central Excise Act, 1944**. 
 
 

• **Objectives of CENVAT:** 
 

• **CENVAT** was introduced to **minimize the cascading effect** of taxes on products and services. 

• It promotes the concept of **value addition taxation**, where tax is applied only to the value added at each stage of production or distribution. 

• The system ensures **better input credit utilization**, allowing manufacturers to claim tax credits on inputs used for production. 
 
 

• **Reforms in Taxation:** 
 

• The rationalization of excise duty in 2001-02 was part of broader reforms to modernize India's taxation system. 

• Other significant reforms include the introduction of VAT (Value Added Tax) and later, the **Goods and Services Tax (GST)** in 2017, which replaced multiple indirect taxes. 

• These reforms aimed to create a **unified and streamlined tax structure** for goods and services. 
 
 

• **Impact of Excise Duty Rationalization:** 
 

• The single rate of **16 per cent CENVAT** reduced administrative complexities for businesses. 

• It encouraged **compliance** and helped manufacturers focus on their operations rather than navigating complex tax structures. 

• It also improved **government revenue collection** by creating a more efficient taxation system.

• This system prevents the cascading effect of taxes and promotes efficiency in the taxation process.

questions.question: The Contingency Fund of an Indian State is held by ________ .
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Governor**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 

• The **Contingency Fund of an Indian State** is established under **Article 267(2)** of the Constitution of India. It is maintained by each state to meet unforeseen expenditures. 

• The fund is placed at the disposal of the **Governor** of the state, who has the authority to make advances out of it to meet urgent and unforeseen expenditures pending authorization by the state legislature. 

• The fund is created by the state legislature through an act, specifying the total amount of the fund. This amount can vary from state to state. 

• The Governor can advance money from the Contingency Fund when immediate action is required, and there is no time to seek approval from the legislature. ***Hence, the correct option is Governor.*** 

• Once the expenditure is incurred, the state government must present it to the legislature for approval, and the amount withdrawn is subsequently recouped into the Contingency Fund. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 

• **Contingency Fund of India:** 
 

• At the Union level, the **Contingency Fund of India** is established under **Article 267(1)** of the Indian Constitution. It is at the disposal of the **President of India**. 

• It is used to meet unforeseen expenses that cannot wait for parliamentary approval. The fund is later replenished by the Parliament. 

• The corpus of the Contingency Fund of India is fixed at **Rs. 500 crore**, as prescribed by the Parliament. 
 
 

• **Difference between Consolidated Fund and Contingency Fund:** 
 

• The **Consolidated Fund** is the main account of the government where all revenues received, loans raised, and money received in repayment of loans are credited. Expenditures from this fund require legislative approval. 

• The **Contingency Fund**, on the other hand, is used for emergency expenditures that cannot wait for legislative approval. 
 
 

• **Role of the Governor in Finances:** 
 

• The Governor is the **constitutional head** of a state and has specific financial powers, including the authority to advance money from the Contingency Fund for urgent matters. 

• He/she acts on the advice of the state council of ministers, headed by the Chief Minister, in financial matters. 
 
 

• **Examples of Contingency Fund Usage:** 
 

• Natural disasters, such as floods, cyclones, or earthquakes, often require immediate financial assistance, which can be drawn from the Contingency Fund. 

• Emergency relief measures during pandemics or public health crises can also utilize this fund. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 

• The Contingency Fund is meant to ensure the smooth functioning of the government in times of financial emergencies. 

• It is a temporary arrangement, and all expenditures must later be approved by the legislature to maintain accountability and transparency. 

• Both the Union and the States in India have their respective Contingency Funds, managed by the President and Governors, respectively. 

• While the Governor has the authority to use the fund, the legislature plays a crucial role in ensuring proper checks and balances by approving or disapproving the expenditures.

questions.question: Which of the following port is confronted with the problem of silt accumulation in the Hugli River?
questions.solution:

__
 
• **Kolkata Port**, officially known as the **Syama Prasad Mukherjee Port**, is located on the banks of the **Hugli River** in West Bengal, India.
 
• The port faces a major challenge due to **silt accumulation** in the Hugli River, which requires frequent dredging to maintain navigability.
 
• The problem of silt accumulation arises because the Hugli River is a distributary of the Ganges, carrying a heavy load of **sediment** deposited in the riverbed.
 
• This sedimentation significantly affects the port's **draft depth**, leading to difficulties in handling large vessels and increasing maintenance costs.
 
• The Kolkata Port relies on continuous dredging operations funded by the **Government of India** to ensure smooth functioning and to prevent disruptions in maritime trade.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• Established in **1870**, it is one of the oldest operating ports in India.
 
• It serves as a crucial trade hub for the eastern and northeastern regions of India.
 
• It has two dock systems: **Kolkata Dock System** (KDS) and **Haldia Dock Complex** (HDC).
 
• The port primarily handles cargo such as **petroleum products, iron ore, fertilizers, and containers**.
 
 
 
• **Silt Accumulation in Hugli River:**
 
 
• The Hugli River is a tidal river, and its sediment load is influenced by the **monsoon season** and tides.
 
• Silt accumulation reduces the **draft depth**, making it challenging for large vessels to navigate.
 
• To combat this, the port authority conducts dredging operations to maintain a minimum draft level of **7 meters**.
 
• This issue is exacerbated by the river's complex **meandering patterns** and the presence of shifting sandbanks.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Ports:**
 
 
• **Kochchi Port:** Located in Kerala, it is a major port on the Arabian Sea and does not face issues of silt accumulation due to its coastal location.
 
• **Tuticorin Port:** Situated in Tamil Nadu, it is a deep-sea port handling large cargo vessels without challenges related to riverine siltation.
 
• **Chennai Port:** Also in Tamil Nadu, it is a coastal port with a natural harbor; it does not require extensive dredging compared to Kolkata Port.
 
 
 
• **Economic Impact:**
 
 
• Silt accumulation increases operational costs due to regular dredging activities, impacting the port's profitability.
 
• It limits the port's ability to handle large vessels, affecting trade efficiency and capacity.
 
• The Government of India allocates significant funds annually to maintain navigability and ensure uninterrupted trade operations.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Hugli River Facts:**

 
 
• The Hugli River is a distributary of the **Ganges River**, flowing through West Bengal.
 
• Its sedimentation is influenced by **seasonal tides** and upstream erosion.
 
• The river is vital for inland trade but poses challenges for maritime navigation due to **sandbank formations**.
 
 
 
• **Dredging Technology:**
 
 
• Dredging involves removing **sediment deposits** to deepen waterways and maintain navigability.
 
• Advanced dredging equipment, such as **trailing suction hopper dredgers**, is employed at Kolkata Port.
 
• Continuous dredging ensures the port remains operational despite the natural sedimentation process.
 
 
 
• **Historical Significance:**
 
 
• Kolkata Port played a crucial role in India's **colonial trade** as the gateway to the Bengal region.
 
• Post-independence, the port has remained a vital hub for **exports and imports** in eastern India.

Its primary objective was to formulate and implement **five-year plans** for the country’s socio-economic development.
 
• The Commission was tasked with assessing the resources of the country and devising strategies to utilize them efficiently for economic growth and development. **Hence, its primary function was to formulate and implement five-year plans.**
 
• The first **Five-Year Plan (1951-56)** focused on the agricultural sector to address food shortages and ensure self-sufficiency. Subsequent plans targeted various sectors like industrialization, poverty alleviation, and infrastructure.
 
• The Planning Commission coordinated between **central and state governments** to ensure the successful implementation of plans and programs, while also monitoring their progress and effectiveness.
 
• It also played a role in allocating resources across different sectors and regions, ensuring balanced development across the country.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• The idea of central planning in India was inspired by the **Soviet Union**, where planning was used as a tool to achieve rapid industrialization and economic development.
 
• The Planning Commission was established on **15 March 1950**, following India's independence in 1947, to fulfill the vision of a planned economy.
 
 
 
• **Features of Five-Year Plans:**
 
 
• The Five-Year Plans were aimed at achieving specific objectives like **economic growth**, poverty reduction, employment generation, and regional balance.
 
• Each plan was based on detailed studies of national priorities and resource availability, ensuring comprehensive coverage of various sectors.
 
• The Planning Commission used a mix of **market mechanisms** and government intervention to achieve developmental goals.
 
 
 
• **Replacement of Planning Commission:**
 
 
• In 2015, the Planning Commission was replaced by the **NITI Aayog** (National Institution for Transforming India) to align planning with the needs of a dynamic economy.
 
• NITI Aayog focuses on **policy formulation, cooperative federalism, and real-time monitoring** of developmental progress instead of fixed five-year plans.
 
 
 
• **Functions of NITI Aayog:**
 
 
• Unlike the Planning Commission, NITI Aayog acts as a think-tank and provides **policy advice** to both central and state governments.
 
• It emphasizes **bottom-up planning** and involves states as equal partners in the development process.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Option 2:** "To boost the foreign trade" is incorrect as foreign trade policies were managed by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, not the Planning Commission.
 
• **Option 4:** "To monitor the currency exchange system in India" is incorrect because this responsibility lies with the **Reserve Bank of India** and not the Planning Commission.
 
• The Planning Commission's focus was on long-term development strategies, resource allocation, and sectoral planning, which makes **Option 3 the correct answer.**
